P1.evidence: Application referenced but not read back. The frame was better than most in this batch because it built in an explicit fit test — 'let's check if we can help you, if Trevor is the one that can actually help you with what you're trying to fix, and we'll take it from there' — which is two of the four parts plus a genuine two-way qualification, and it is the frame the rep actually acted on later when he disqualified the prospect. Still no where-you-want-to-go or what-you-need element, and agreement was only a trailing 'Yeah, perfect.' The open question ran cleanly.

P2.evidence: Four hits and a familiar shape of gaps. Injuries asked directly and cleanly — 'Do you have any injuries from the past, or anything that limits your movements, actually?' — and answered clear, which is what made the later fit judgement defensible. Training week established in detail: six or seven days a week, three or four kettlebell sessions plus running, swimming and cycling. Results from current training asked well — 'you've already done some good work. So what would make this even better?' — which is a good question and the pivot point of the whole call. Diet walked through thoroughly including alcohol, which surfaced the two-glasses-a-night habit he had recently dropped. Against that: no age, no height, no weight anywhere; health conditions never asked; sleep never asked despite the prospect twice linking alcohol to sleep quality; and occupation volunteered rather than asked, with the rep's follow-up questions going to where he lives rather than what the work demands of him.

P3.evidence: The goal question was asked — 'do you have like any particular goal that you would like to hit?' — and answered 'No, not really', which is where a lot of reps would stop. This one did not, and the prospect then produced the real material unprompted: feeling good and confident at work, being energised around his daughter, and 'to be more in the shape I was when I first met her.' The legacy thread is the strongest part and the rep drove it deliberately, from 'Son or daughter?' through 'You want to be the active dad when you're 62' and the Brazilian hiking anecdote, drawing a genuine response — 'someone she can be proud of too. I mean, it's not just a physical appearance thing.' What never ran: no bridge question, no 'what does moving better do for you', no can't-do question, and the who-else-does-this-impact link was supplied by the rep rather than drawn out. Reflect-back was light — 'Super dad for your daughter' — and never tested the deeper why back to him.

P4.evidence: The best-run root cause phase in the batch. The why-did-it-stop question was asked directly and early, which almost never happens: 'Why is that? Like, it's like, if you were an athlete, why did you stop?' It produced the honest answer about the business, the child and living away from family, and the prospect's own verdict on it. What happened with the alternatives was established — YouTube content that 'can often feel a bit cookie cutter' and 'it just feels a bit random.' The blocker was named and confirmed as structure. And the rep delivered P4f properly, in his own words rather than the script's: 'you can find almost everything online right now. The tricky part is to actually put it all together and that it's going to be tailored to your needs, to your schedule, to your lifestyle.' The prospect then closed the loop himself — 'I don't have the skills, quite frankly, Andrew... it's just not my forte to go and do the structure of a workout.' That is the phase working exactly as intended.

P5.evidence: Never run. No two-year projection, no settle question, no 'why not', no line in the sand. Ten calls into this batch and the consequence frame has not been attempted once. The prospect handed over the obvious opening himself — 'it's when it gets busy that I need to stay motivated... it's too easy to make excuses' — and nothing was built on it.

P6.evidence: The belief question ran in near-scripted form and got an unambiguous answer — 'do you personally feel like this can get you to your goals?' / 'Yeah, yeah, absolutely' — but it ran after the delay had been conceded, as part of the spouse play, rather than before presenting. The all-in question never ran. P6c is partial by an unusual route: the rep moved to a recommendation without a commitment check, but the recommendation was a disqualification rather than a close, so the sequence broke in a direction the script does not contemplate.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted — 'we'll go over the payment. I'll get you onboarded and you're ready to go. You will have access right now. So you can start your workout even today' — and none of it completed. No payment, no link, no agreement, no onboarding scheduled beyond a proposed five-to-ten-minute call on Monday. The rep had a buyer who had said money was not an obstacle, that his wife had no reason to object, and that there was no universe in which she said no, and still finished the call with details to be emailed.

objection_plays.detail: The most complete spouse play in this batch and it still lost the close. Four moves ran, in a sensible order. He offered a clean out first — 'it's a yes or no, like, if the money is tied, just let me know, it's totally fine.' He ran the belief question: 'do you personally feel like this can get you to your goals?' He ran the would-she-object move: 'When you talk to her, do you feel she'd want you to get back in shape?' He ran the obstacles move: 'what potential obstacles might be, apart from the finances?' And he added a good variant of his own: 'is there, like, a universe that she would potentially say no?' Every answer came back clean — no financial obstacle, no obstacle at all, no universe where she says no, purely a courtesy. The rep then correctly diagnosed it out loud — 'So you're just letting her know, basically' — and did nothing with the diagnosis. Having established there was no objection, he did not ask for the sale, ran no deposit fallback, and closed with 'Look, I don't want you to sleep on a couch because of that.' The play was executed and then abandoned one move from the finish.

A think-about-it trigger sat alongside the spouse objection — 'give me just the weekend to think about it' and 'just kind of spend the weekend and just make sure I'm comfortable.' None of the OA moves ran. No 'what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started', no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no different-decision or identity move, no final 'are you sure, nothing else keeping you from being 100% in.' The rep's de-pressure line — 'we don't need to take three days to think about it' — pointed the right way and was immediately dropped.

SCRIPT GAP, and the most consequential one in this batch — the rep's own decision to disqualify a prospect from the flagship product. 'I want to be honest with you, because my goal is to direct you in a way that is going to be best tailored to your needs... from what I'm hearing, you don't need one-on-one with Trevor... I think pitching you, working with Trevor, which is like a premium solution, it's not the right fit.' There is no guidance anywhere in the playbook on when a prospect should be steered down, who decides, or whether the premium price should be named before the recommendation is made. Here it was not: the $6,000 figure was never spoken, so the prospect could not weigh the choice himself. The reasoning was sound and honestly delivered, and the rep supported it with a full upgrade-credit commitment. But the same rep withheld a cheaper tier from Patrick Dominguez two days earlier to steer that buyer up. Both calls have the rep unilaterally selecting which tier the customer sees, and the playbook is silent on it.

notes: P4 was the best-executed root cause work in the batch and the discovery genuinely earned the fit judgement — the injury question was asked and came back clear, the training week was established, and the prospect said outright that motivation is not his problem. Two things to take to the principal rather than to coaching. First, a five-out-of-five ICP match with no financial constraint was moved off a $6,000 product onto a $1,000 one without ever hearing the higher price; whether or not that was the right call, the rule for making it needs to exist and be written down. Second, the spouse play ran almost perfectly, established there was no objection at all, and then simply stopped — after 'is there a universe where she says no?' comes back 'No, not really', the next line is an ask, not a goodbye.
